panorama_meta.title: Curiosity's First 360-Degree View of Boxwork Patterns

properties.science: Curiosity's first 360-degree Mastcam station inside the Mount Sharp boxwork formations (site 116, sols 4539–4541). Crisscrossing low ridges (~1–2 m tall) formed where ancient groundwater flowed through bedrock fractures, precipitating calcium-sulfate minerals that resisted wind erosion better than the surrounding host rock. Hosted within the CRISM-mapped polyhydrated/monohydrated sulfate unit (boxwork texture is resolved by Curiosity surface imaging, below CRISM's 18 m/px orbital resolution).

panorama_meta.title: Curiosity Captures a 360-Degree View at Nevado Sajama

properties.science: Ridgetop panorama and drill station at 'Nevado Sajama' inside the boxwork unit (site 120). A 1.5-gigapixel mosaic stitched from 1,031 Mastcam right-eye (100 mm) frames captured across sols 4714–4741, showing polygonal fracture ridges and hollows across lower Mount Sharp, paired with nighttime LED-lit MAHLI inspection of the drill borehole wall.

properties.science: First rotary-percussive drill sample collected inside the Mount Sharp boxwork unit (drilled June 8, 2025; JPL release June 23, 2025). Powdered bedrock from 'Altadena' was delivered to Curiosity's internal CheMin (X-ray diffraction) and SAM (gas chromatograph / mass spectrometer) laboratories to analyze the cement mineralogy and test how ancient groundwater evolved as Gale Crater dried out.

properties.science: Curiosity's 44th Martian drill target, sampled inside the 'Monte Grande' hollow—a less-resistant bedrock depression bounded by hardened boxwork ridges (sols 4689–4694, October 2025). Comparing hollow bedrock at Valle de la Luna against ridge-crest targets tests why mineral-cemented fractures resisted erosion while intervening hollows weathered away.
